title: Nectar robbing from Hibiscus flowers by White-eyes on an oceanic island, Chichi-jima, Bonin Islands
decision_basis: Primary field study measures flower size independently and reports a quantitative robbed-versus-unrobbed size association; larger flowers were robbed more often. Reward covariation is retained as a causal limitation rather than used to exclude the direct empirical relation.
notes: Eligibility frozen before direction coding; flower size is a geometry predictor but nectar reward covaries with size.

title: Geographic Variation in Flower Size and Flower-Visitor Composition of Two Bumblebee-Pollinated, Spring-Flowering Herbs, Lamium album L. var. barbatum (Lamiaceae) and Meehania urticifolia (Lamiaceae)
decision_basis: Primary study measures Meehania calyx length and width independently and fits a binomial-logit GLM for robber bite-mark presence using CL, CW and CL×CW; CW and the interaction are significant.
notes: Eligibility frozen before direction coding; direction remains unresolved because published test statistics do not give coefficient signs for CW and CL×CW.

title: Reproductive success and production of nectar in Mandevilla funiformis (Apocynaceae): accessibility to visitors and effect of floral stage
decision_basis: Primary study measures floral morphology and records robbers/thieves, nectar and reproduction, but no recoverable quantitative comparison/model uses an independently measured access-geometry variable to predict route-resolved robbery.
notes: Retain as floral-biology context, not a formal geometry-to-robbery directional test.

title: Blueberry floral morphology influences pollinator visitation and behavioural patterns
decision_basis: Primary study tests cultivar effects on percentage robbed and separately models flower-size PC1 against visitation behaviour of the main visitors; the reported robbery differences are not a direct model/comparison with geometry as the robbery predictor under the frozen contract.
notes: The discussion associates restrictive morphology with robbing, but the formal direct-test gate requires the geometry-to-robbery relation itself to be quantitatively estimated.
